new_statements.quote: Analyzing accent marks in Li’s materials reveals a preference for penultimate stress in Wailaki. Li’s description of Wailaki stress is consistent with an analysis whereby penultimate stress is preferred if one assumes heavy stems still have penultimate stress, even if word-final on the surface, due to the presence of an underlying relative enclitic, or another enclitic, which may often be deleted. Li also writes an accent mark over syllables in other positions on occasion, but the predominant pattern is penultimate stress. [p. 66] ... For each length, the proportion that has penultimate stress is at least 65%. [...] Considered overall, however, the figure is higher: 79.6% [...] Despite these outstanding questions, the preference for penultimate stress is clear in the data. [p. 68]

new_statements.locator: §2.7 Stress, pp. 66 and 68 (PDF pp. 77, 79); Table 14 p. 68
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (288 pp., eScholarship title page: 'Wailaki Grammar', Kayla Rae Begay, UC Berkeley, Fall 2017, (c) 2017, eScholarship publication date 2018; so Glottolog's 2017 is the dissertation date and 2018 the online date) and the companion. Section '2.7 Stress' starts on printed p. 66 = PDF p. 77 and runs to printed p. 68 = PDF p. 79, exactly as the locator says. All three quoted passages are there verbatim: 'Analyzing accent marks in Li's materials reveals a preference for penultimate stress in Wailaki. Li's description of Wailaki stress is consistent with an analysis whereby penultimate stress is preferred if one assumes heavy stems still have penultimate stress, even if word-final on the su…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (79.6% of 1363 stress-marked tokens in Li's 1927 notecards; two-syllable words 84.5% initial, three-syllable 82.6% second, four-syllable 74.5% third, five-syllable 68.4% fourth). Li's older rule (stress on the stem if heavy, on the syllable before the stem if light) is treated as penultimate stress with a deleted word-final enclitic. No lexical tone; Wailaki has a stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; about 1.5% of tokens are 'double marked' (two accent marks, on two prefixes or a prefix and the stem) and are left unexplained.
new_statements.exceptions: About 20% of tokens carry stress outside the penult; the conditioning factors (syllable weight, weight hierarchy, noun vs. verb) are explicitly left for further research. Phonetic correlates unknown since no recordings exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based entirely on philological analysis of accent marks in Fang-Kuei Li's 1927 field notecards (431 cards, mostly verb paradigms and wordlist forms), i.e. citation/elicited forms of a dormant language; no acoustic data.
new_statements.identity_note: Begay 2018 uses 'Wailaki' as a cover term for the whole Eel River Athabaskan dialect continuum (Glottolog wail1244, ISO wlk; Golla 2011's Eel River Athabaskan, incl. Wailaki proper, Lassik, Nongatl, Sinkyone); the stress analysis rests on Li's 1927 data from Round Valley speakers (Wailaki proper). Cahto/Kato is a separate language and is not covered.

new_statements.quote: Li (1930:22) briefly considers Wailkai stress in his Mattole grammar. Li considered Wailaki to have a stress system rather than lexical tone, and wrote that an “accent mark in Hupa, Wailaki and Mattole denote stress” (Li 1930: 5). Li also noted a correlation with heavy and light stem forms, writing that “in Wailaki the distinction of heavy and light forms in this case lies in the accent, on the stem if heavy and on the syllable preceding the stem if light…” [...] Analyzing accent marks in Li’s materials reveals a preference for penultimate stress in Wailaki. [...] For each length, the proportion that has penultimate stress is at least 65%. [...] Considered overall, however, the figure is higher: 79.6%

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as catalog record 'Wailaki penultimate stress (penultimate at every length) and identical to the existing_statement already drawn from this work; adds the per-length percentages, the heavy/light stem correlation from Li 1930:22, the double-marked residue and the caveat that ~20% of Li's tokens are marked elsewhere.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. In Li's 1927 notecards (1363 stress-marked tokens), penultimate marking is 84.5% for 2-syllable words, 82.6% for 3, 74.5% for 4, 68.4% for 5, and the majority for 6-7; 79.6% overall. Stems that surface with final stress (heavy stems) are analysed as still penultimate because of an underlying (often deleted) enclitic. Li 1930:22 (as quoted): accent on the stem if the stem form is heavy, on the syllable preceding the stem if light. No lexical tone; correlates of stress unknown (no recordings).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; Begay notes 21 tokens (1.5%) 'double marked' (two accent marks, prefix+prefix or prefix+stem) whose status is unexplained.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress marked outside the penult in roughly 20% of tokens; motivating factors 'unknown, and require further examination' (syllable weight, weight hierarchy, word class noun vs verb named as open questions). Heavy-stem forms with surface-final stress are treated as penultimate via an underlying enclitic.
new_statements.identity_note: Begay 2018 describes Eel River Wailaki (Tsennahkennes), the most documented of the four regional Wailaki dialects; the stress counts come from Li Fang-Kuei's 1927 notecards from speaker John 'Wylakke' Tip, Round Valley Reservation. Li 1930 is a grammar of Mattole (Mattole-Bear River, a different Eel River Athabaskan language); only its pp. 5 and 22 comment on Wailaki.

sources.note: Section 2.7 'Stress' (pp. 66-68): no audio exists; analysis of accent marks in Li Fang-Kuei's 1927 notecards (1363 stress-marked tokens) shows a clear preference for penultimate stress (79.6% overall; >=65% for every word length); Li's heavy/light stem rule (stress on stem if heavy, on syllable before stem if light) is reconciled with penultimacy via a deleted enclitic; no lexical tone; factors for non-penultimate placement (weight, word class) left open.
